Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[ja:%E5%B7%9D%E5%86%85%E5%85%AB%E5%B9%A1%E5%AE%AE%E4%BE%8B%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%AD]] [[sn:Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]]

'''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival''' {{Image requested|Climax, Sacred Object, Mioshi Curtain|date=September 2023|cat=Mutsu City}} '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival''' (かわうちはちまんぐうれいたいさい) is the annual festival of '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine''', located in '''Kawauchi Town, Mutsu City, Aomori Prefecture, Japan'''. It is also called '''"Kawauchi Festival"''' (かわうちまつり). The festival has been designated as an '''Aomori Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property'''{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.aomori.lg.jp/soshiki/kyoiku/e-bunka/kenmukei_43.html |title=Aomori Prefecture - Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kawauchi's Dashi Procession |publisher=Aomori Prefecture |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. This festival is part of the '''Gion Matsuri tradition''', originating from Kyoto, and features '''large wooden dashi (festival floats)''' over '''5 meters''' in height. These '''fixed wooden floats''' are among the largest in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' and even within '''Aomori Prefecture'''.

Note: Variations in pronunciation and dialectal expressions by editors remain. Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[ja:%E5%B7%9D%E5%86%85%E5%85%AB%E5%B9%A1%E5%AE%AE%E4%BE%8B%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%AD]] [[sn:Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals of Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]]

During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[ja:%E5%B7%9D%E5%86%85%E5%85%AB%E5%B9%A1%E5%AE%AE%E4%BE%8B%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%AD]] [[sn:Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[Category:paes with no wikidata]] [[Category:paes with no wikidata]]

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry (none) Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:28, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|Wikidata entry (none) Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 04:07, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival''' {{Image requested|Climax, Sacred Object, Mioshi Curtain|date=September 2023|cat=Mutsu City}} '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival''' (かわうちはちまんぐうれいたいさい) is the annual festival of '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine''', located in '''Kawauchi Town, Mutsu City, Aomori Prefecture, Japan'''. It is also called '''"Kawauchi Festival"''' (かわうちまつり). The festival has been designated as an '''Aomori Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property'''{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.aomori.lg.jp/soshiki/kyoiku/e-bunka/kenmukei_43.html |title=Aomori Prefecture - Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kawauchi's Dashi Procession |publisher=Aomori Prefecture |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. This festival is part of the '''Gion Matsuri tradition''', originating from Kyoto, and features '''large wooden dashi (festival floats)''' over '''5 meters''' in height. These '''fixed wooden floats''' are among the largest in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' and even within '''Aomori Prefecture'''.

Note: Variations in pronunciation and dialectal expressions by editors remain. Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[sn:E5%B7%9D%E5%86%85%E5%85%AB%E5%B9%A1%E5%AE%AE%E4%BE%8B%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%AD]] [[sn:Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[Category:paes with no wikidata]] [[Category:paes with no wikidata]]

Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[sn:E5%B7%9D%E5%86%85%E5%85%AB%E5%B9%A1%E5%AE%AE%E4%BE%8B%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%AD]] [[sn:Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[Category:pages without english wikidata name]]

This festival is part of the '''Gion Matsuri tradition''', originating from Kyoto, and features '''large wooden dashi (festival floats)''' over '''5 meters''' in height. These '''fixed wooden floats''' are among the largest in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' and even within '''Aomori Prefecture'''.

Note: Variations in pronunciation and dialectal expressions by editors remain. Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[sn:E5%B7%9D%E5%86%85%E5%85%AB%E5%B9%A1%E5%AE%AE%E4%BE%8B%E5%A4%A7%E7%A5%AD]] [[sn:Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[Category:pages without english wikidata name]] {{wikidata link|Q132449332}}

Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] {{wikidata link|Q132449332}}

Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] {{wikidata link|Q132449332}} [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Wikidata no English label]]

These '''fixed wooden floats''' are among the largest in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' and even within '''Aomori Prefecture'''.

Note: Variations in pronunciation and dialectal expressions by editors remain. Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Completion tier 3]] }} [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] {{wikidata link|Q132449332}} [[Category:Wikidata no short description]] [[Category:Wikidata no English label]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]][[Category:LINKED FROM WIKIDATA DO NOT OVERWRITE]]

[[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q132449332]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 05:17, 12 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|Wikidata entry (none) Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:28, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{afc comment|Wikidata entry (none) Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 04:07, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival''' {{Image requested|Climax, Sacred Object, Mioshi Curtain|date=September 2023|cat=Mutsu City}} '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival''' (かわうちはちまんぐうれいたいさい) is the annual festival of '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine''', located in '''Kawauchi Town, Mutsu City, Aomori Prefecture, Japan'''. It is also called '''"Kawauchi Festival"''' (かわうちまつり). The festival has been designated as an '''Aomori Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property'''{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.aomori.lg.jp/soshiki/kyoiku/e-bunka/kenmukei_43.html |title=Aomori Prefecture - Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kawauchi's Dashi Procession |publisher=Aomori Prefecture |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. This festival is part of the '''Gion Matsuri tradition''', originating from Kyoto, and features '''large wooden dashi (festival floats)''' over '''5 meters''' in height. These '''fixed wooden floats''' are among the largest in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' and even within '''Aomori Prefecture'''.

Note: Variations in pronunciation and dialectal expressions by editors remain. Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| }} [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] {{wikidata link|Q132449332}} [[Category:Completion tier 3]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Wikidata no English label]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]]

[[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival''' {{Image requested|Climax, Sacred Object, Mioshi Curtain|date=September 2023|cat=Mutsu City}} '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival''' (かわうちはちまんぐうれいたいさい) is the annual festival of '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine''', located in '''Kawauchi Town, Mutsu City, Aomori Prefecture, Japan'''. It is also called '''"Kawauchi Festival"''' (かわうちまつり). The festival has been designated as an '''Aomori Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property'''{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.aomori.lg.jp/soshiki/kyoiku/e-bunka/kenmukei_43.html |title=Aomori Prefecture - Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kawauchi's Dashi Procession |publisher=Aomori Prefecture |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. This festival is part of the '''Gion Matsuri tradition''', originating from Kyoto, and features '''large wooden dashi (festival floats)''' over '''5 meters''' in height. These '''fixed wooden floats''' are among the largest in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' and even within '''Aomori Prefecture'''.

Note: Variations in pronunciation and dialectal expressions by editors remain. Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[ja:川内八幡宮例大祭]] {{wikidata link|Q132449332}} [[Category:Completion tier 3]] [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Wikidata no English label]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]]

'''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine Festival''' {{Image requested|Climax, Sacred Object, Mioshi Curtain|date=September 2023|cat=Mutsu City}} '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival''' (かわうちはちまんぐうれいたいさい) is the annual festival of '''Kawauchi Hachimangu Shrine''', located in '''Kawauchi Town, Mutsu City, Aomori Prefecture, Japan'''. It is also called '''"Kawauchi Festival"''' (かわうちまつり). The festival has been designated as an '''Aomori Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property'''{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.aomori.lg.jp/soshiki/kyoiku/e-bunka/kenmukei_43.html |title=Aomori Prefecture - Prefectural Intangible Folk Cultural Property: Kawauchi's Dashi Procession |publisher=Aomori Prefecture |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. This festival is part of the '''Gion Matsuri tradition''', originating from Kyoto, and features '''large wooden dashi (festival floats)''' over '''5 meters''' in height. These '''fixed wooden floats''' are among the largest in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' and even within '''Aomori Prefecture'''.

Note: Variations in pronunciation and dialectal expressions by editors remain. Some expressions have been left in their original dialect for authenticity. == History & Background == The participation of '''dashi (festival floats)''' in the Kawauchi Hachimangu Grand Festival{{refnest|group="Note"|The grand festival ('''reitaisai''') is the most important festival of each shrine{{Cite web |url=https://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/omatsuri/jinja_no_omatsuri/jinjanoomatsuritoha |title=What is a Shrine Festival? |publisher=Jinja Honcho (Association of Shinto Shrines) |accessdate=September 7, 2023}}. Some major grand festivals have historical records of lavish dashi participation. However, these festivals initially began as '''religious ceremonies''' at shrines, with dashi participation being a later addition by parishioners.}} is historically significant in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita region'''. It is believed that '''by the first year of Shōtoku (1711)''', '''dashi floats''' were already part of the '''Hachimangu Grand Festival''', making it one of the oldest float festivals in the regionMany shrines in the '''Mutsu-Shimokita area''' also have historical records of dashi participation from the same period, such as '''Ōhata District (Kyōhō 3, 1718)'''.. Since the '''Edo period''', the region had strong ties to the '''Kitamaebune trading routes''', facilitating cultural exchanges with various parts of JapanThis exchange was not limited to '''Ōmi merchants''', as '''West Japan's maritime trade''' gradually shifted to a '''San'in and Setouchi route''', bringing influences from '''Noto Peninsula, Setouchi, and even Kyoto'''.. As a result, influences from '''Kyoto's Gion Festival, regional festival music, and other cultural elements''' were transmitted to this area. Even influences from the '''Tōkai region, the Hokuriku area, and distant Osaka Bay''' can be seen in the '''festival's dashi structures and musical styles'''. The '''daytime decorations''' of the floats are luxurious, influenced by Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', featuring '''embroidered fabrics and foreign materials such as Persian rugs'''. Meanwhile, the '''night decorations''' incorporate '''painted illuminated panels''', influenced by the '''Nebuta Festival''' from the '''Tsugaru region'''. Details on these elements are covered in the section '''"Kagura & Dashi"'''. During the '''Taishō period''', the '''economic prosperity of Kawauchi temporarily surpassed that of Tanabu'''{{Citation |title=Development and Decline: The Untold History of Abejo Mine |periodical=Mutsu Chamber of Commerce Report |number=August 1, 2013 |url=http://www.mutsucci.or.jp/kaiho/pdf/kai184.pdf |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}, potentially leading to '''further expansion of the dashi'''. This might have contributed to the '''festival's later reputation as a "fighting festival" (喧嘩祭り, Kenka Matsuri)''' due to disputes over float operations. Originally held on the '''lunar calendar's 15th of August''', the festival was moved to '''September 14-15''' after the '''Meiji Restoration''', and later shifted to the '''weekend before Respect for the Aged Day (Keirō no Hi) from 2004 onward'''{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2003-2.htm |title=2003 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}{{Cite web |url=http://iwagei.com/koyomi2004-2.htm |title=2004 Folk Performing Arts Calendar |work=Iwate Prefecture Folk Arts |accessdate=August 13, 2023}}. == Overview == * The festival parade consists of: ''' '''Sarutahiko (deity guide)''' ''' '''Yachicho Daikagura''' ''' '''Chigo Procession (child participants, only during the daytime)''' ''' '''Hachimangu Mikoshi (portable shrine)''' ''' '''Surrounding villages’ kagura (1 unit, varies annually)''' ''' '''Five major festival floats (dashi)''' * The dashi (festival floats) are '''two-story, roofed wooden structures''', inspired by '''Kyoto's Gion Festival's hoko-yama (peak floats) but without spears'''. The '''first level houses musicians''', while the '''second level enshrines sacred objects'''. * Each float has '''wooden wheels''' reinforced with '''iron rims''' to prevent breakage. However, '''they lack steering mechanisms''', making turns difficult. ''' '''"Kaji-bō" (rudder poles)''' are used for direction control. ''' '''"Tego" (lever tools)''' assist in movement adjustments. ''' Unlike Kyoto’s '''Gion Festival''', '''no bamboo slats are used for turning'''. ''' '''Electric cables''' obstructing the path are lifted with '''a specialized tool resembling a TV antenna'''. * The '''floats are pulled by ropes''', and their decorations change between '''daytime and nighttime'''. ''' '''Daytime:''' Features '''banners, front panels, embroidered curtains, and sacred decorations'''. ''' '''Nighttime:''' Features '''painted illuminated panels''', replacing '''daytime banners'''. == Highlights & Climax == * The '''river crossing (Yanma Yāre)''' and '''final large-scale performances (Iyo-iya Sassa)''' are the festival's highlights. * The '''"fighting festival" reputation''' originates from historical '''accidental collisions''' between large floats. * In the '''grand finale''', two floats often '''face off in a performance duel'''. ==Referenes== {{translated page|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭|version=101692431|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{wikidata link|Q132449332|ja|川内八幡宮例大祭}} [[Category:Festivals in Aomori Prefecture]] [[Category:Float festivals of Japan]] [[Category:Image Requests for Mutsu City]] [[Category:Mutsu, Aomori]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Wikidata no English label]] [[Category:Wikidata no short description]]
